narrative:
The model estimated a 52.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but because it crosses the rejection threshold used here, your law school application was denied; it is a risk forecast, not a statement that you cannot succeed. Your gender and race were not factors.

The strongest reason for the denial was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That low standing pushed the prediction toward failure. The next most influential factor was your LSAT score of 39, which was above the accepted-student average of about 37 and therefore pushed toward passing. Even so, it was not enough to overcome the academic-standing signal. The third factor was your first-year class standing, also the lowest decile versus an average near the sixth decile, which again pushed toward failure.

To move forward, request a human review of the decision and explain any context behind your early class ranks. Ask what conditional admission or academic-support options exist, and work with an advisor on a concrete bar-preparation plan. You may also consider strengthening your record before reapplying, while emphasizing your solid LSAT and undergraduate GPA.
